india-deep-tech-178d0227a0.headline: Design, develop & deploy: Sarvam signs 5-year MoU with MoD to build AI for Army, Navy, IAF
india-deep-tech-178d0227a0.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint
india-deep-tech-178d0227a0.fulltext:
New Delhi: Bengaluru-based AI company Sarvam has signed a five-year memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff (HQ IDS), Ministry of Defence, setting up an umbrella framework for artificial intelligence projects across the Indian Army, Navy and Air Force.
HQ IDS announced the MoU on 26 October, and the company made it public Tuesday. In a post on X, the defence ministry said the two sides would collaborate “on AI applications, research, knowledge management, training and decision-support” across the three services.
HQ IDS was set up in 2001 following the recommendations of the Kargil Review Committee to coordinate planning and operations among the three services. The framework extends to the joint, tri-service and integrated organisations under it.
Under the pact, Sarvam will design, develop and deploy AI applications for the operational, training and decision-support requirements of the services and provide follow-on technical support, while HQ IDS will facilitate the engagement.
A significant step towards strengthening sovereign AI capabilities for India’s Defence Forces.
HQ Integrated Defence Staff and Sarvam #AI have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to collaborate on AI applications, research, knowledge management, training and decision-support… pic.twitter.com/GLKYWUDZMu
— HQ Integrated Def Staff (@HQ_IDS_India) October 26, 2026
According to the company, the services and joint organisations will get access to the same foundation models, agentic infrastructure, and geospatial and perception systems, so that doctrine and lessons from one service’s projects can feed into the next.
The focus areas are decision support, target acquisition and data fusion across the “sensor-to-shooter loop”—the chain from detecting a target to engaging it—with human oversight retained on operational decisions.
Sarvam said the AI layer would be built in India and deployed on sovereign infrastructure. Projects under the MoU include an “AI fabric” that connects the elements of India’s defence capabilities.
“Sarvam exists to build AI in India, for India,” said Pratyush Kumar, co-founder, Sarvam. He described working with the three services as “an honour and a privilege”, and thanked HQ IDS for its trust.
Neither side disclosed the financial terms, the number of projects or a timeline for deployment.
The work will be carried out by Chanakya, which Sarvam describes as its firewalled division for national security and defence. Sarvam announced Chanakya on 29 March this year, saying the team would work on on-premise deployments in air-gapped setups, multimodal data ingestion and agent-based workflows. Air-gapped systems are cut off from the internet, a requirement for classified military networks.
Chanakya will use Sarvam’s AI stack, including Sarvam 105B, a foundation model the company open-sourced in February. The model uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture, in which only 10.3 billion of its 105 billion parameters are active at a time. It was launched at the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi along with a 30-billion-parameter model, with support for 22 Indian languages.
The MoU builds on Sarvam’s work with a military training institution.
On 18 August, the Defence Services Staff College (DSSC), Wellington, launched DRONA 2.0, a generative AI platform for training, research and strategic studies that runs on Sarvam 105B along with open-source models.
DRONA, short for DSSC Resource Optimising Neural AI, was first launched on the college’s network on 16 June, 2025.
On 18 August, Lt Gen Manish Erry, Commandant, DSSC, launched the upgraded version in the presence of Sarvam co-founder Vivek Raghavan, and the two sides signed an MoU for further development of the platform and other AI applications. The system is hosted on a GPU server within the college’s secure network and was certified by HQ IDS and the Defence Cyber Agency after security audits.
Founded in 2023 by Raghavan and Kumar, Sarvam was selected in 2025 to build India’s sovereign AI model under the IndiaAI Mission. In June, it raised $234 million in the first close of its $300 million Series B round at a post-money valuation of $1.5 billion, with HCLTech investing $150 million as lead strategic investor. In August, it raised another $74 million from Nvidia, Activate, Glade Brook Capital and Gaja Capital to complete the round.
The company linked the latest agreement to the government’s push for ‘Atmanirbharta’ in defence and the indigenisation of defence equipment, which it said now extends to AI. The ministry’s work on military AI predates the pact: a 2019 executive order created the Defence AI Council and the Defence AI Project Agency, and an AI roadmap identifying 70 projects was drawn up for defence public sector undertakings.
Private firms have since moved into the space. According to startup data platform Inc42, 89 percent of Indian defence tech startups report integrating AI into their offerings, as demand rises for autonomous systems, surveillance and communications built in the country.

ai-4ed0d40e6c.headline: US DOJ flags competition risks in Nvidia’s acquisition of open-source AI platform Hugging Face
ai-4ed0d40e6c.fulltext:
US DOJ flags competition risks in Nvidia’s acquisition of open-source AI platform Hugging Face. (Photo: Reuters)
Nvidia’s plan to buy open-source AI platform Hugging Face for $12.93 billion has drawn scrutiny from US regulators, who are examining whether the deal could give the chipmaker an unfair advantage over rivals, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has asked questions about how the proposed acquisition could affect competition in artificial intelligence, including whether it would give Nvidia greater control over an important platform for distributing AI models and tools, the report said.
The inquiry comes as Nvidia faces wider scrutiny of its acquisitions, investments, sales practices and dealings with customers. The company has become a major force in the AI industry, supplying chips used to train and run AI systems while investing in businesses across the sector.
Nvidia has said the Hugging Face deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027. It has also said the platform would continue to support a range of chipmakers, cloud providers and AI companies.
The DOJ’s questions do not establish wrongdoing, and the investigation may not lead to legal action.
Hugging Face operates a widely used platform where developers and researchers share and access AI models, datasets and software tools. Its platform connects developers, businesses and researchers working on artificial intelligence.
Nvidia, meanwhile, is best known for its graphics processing units (GPUs), which power many of the world's leading AI systems, including OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude.
The acquisition could bring Nvidia closer to the developers who build AI applications, extending its reach beyond the hardware used to run them.
However, the DOJ is examining whether ownership of the platform could give Nvidia an advantage over competing chipmakers and AI providers. Officials have reportedly asked how the company might use the acquisition to harm rivals and have also sought information about Hugging Face's competitors.
One concern is whether developers would continue to have meaningful access to alternative hardware and cloud services if the deal goes through.
Nvidia has said Hugging Face would continue to work with a range of providers. The regulatory inquiry will examine potential competition risks, rather than establish that the company intends to restrict access.
The Hugging Face inquiry is part of a broader examination of Nvidia's business practices, according to Reuters.
The DOJ has also examined Nvidia's 2025 arrangement involving AI chip startup Groq, under which Nvidia licensed technology and hired engineers. Officials have explored whether Nvidia offered customers larger allocations of AI chips if they also purchased its networking equipment and Groq processors, Reuters reported.
Such practices can raise competition concerns if a company uses its strength in one market to gain an unfair advantage in another.
The department has also scrutinised Nvidia's acquisition of Run, which makes software that helps AI chips run more efficiently.
Another transaction under examination is Nvidia's December 2025 acquisition of SchedMD, the company behind open-source software used to manage workloads on high-performance computing systems. The software is also used in supercomputing systems relevant to national security.
Nvidia has benefited from growing demand for computing power as technology companies invest heavily in AI models and data centres.
However, rivals are working to reduce their dependence on Nvidia's hardware. Broadcom and Alphabet's Google are developing processors designed for specific computing tasks, while Advanced Micro Devices has pursued deals with AI laboratories and cloud computing companies.
The DOJ's scrutiny raises questions about whether Nvidia's expanding presence across hardware and software could make it harder for competitors to gain ground.
The broader examination began under former US President Joe Biden and has continued under President Donald Trump. Reuters reported that there was no indication Trump had personally intervened in the inquiry.

ai-37f5357ffc.headline: AI agents hacked Anthropic, maker of arguably the most capable AI models for cyberdefense
ai-37f5357ffc.fulltext:
AI agents hacked Anthropic, maker of arguably the most capable AI models for cyberdefense
Key Points
- Cybersecurity startup Cathedral used AI agents to break into Anthropic's internal systems through third-party business software as part of the Claude developer's own bug bounty program.
- Cathedral says AI agents found Slack messages, salary data, and other internal records within hours. Anthropic says the attempts lasted several days and insists that source code and model weights were never exposed.
- The incident shows a growing threat: AI agents can now probe corporate networks around the clock at minimal cost, and even Anthropic isn't safe.
Cybersecurity startup Cathedral used AI agents to infiltrate Anthropic's internal systems through third-party business software, exploiting the AI lab's own bug bounty program to expose major vulnerabilities.
Cathedral reported its access to internal data and messaging systems in a draft report reviewed by The Washington Post. The startup, founded by former employees of DOGE, the U.S. government efficiency agency, sells AI-powered security tools to government agencies and businesses.
Cathedral's researchers got in through external admin and sales programs. According to their report, AI agents running advanced models found paths to meeting transcripts, salary data, job postings, and Slack messages in under twelve hours.
Anthropic confirmed that the researchers accessed a limited set of sales, human resources, and IT systems, including contact information for some customers and partners along with basic user account data. Chats with Claude, source code, and model weights were never exposed, the company said. Anthropic shut down the affected access points the same day it found the breach, disabled the third-party programs until the issue was resolved, and notified U.S. federal authorities.
Anthropic and Cathedral disagree on how long the breach lasted and how far it reached
Cathedral says the incident took less than twelve hours. Anthropic says the attempted attack stretched over several days. Only after days of probing Anthropic's own systems did the startup pivot to third-party software, according to Anthropic red teamer Logan Graham. There, Cathedral found two vulnerabilities but reported only one. Anthropic says it discovered and patched the second on its own.
Anthropic also accuses Cathedral of violating the bug bounty program's rules through incomplete disclosure. Graham added that targeting third-party providers and pulling data went beyond the program's safe harbor provisions, though he welcomed the discovery of the vulnerabilities. Cathedral maintains it followed standard security research practices.
How much data was actually accessed is still disputed. Former OpenAI employee Will Depue has claimed that Anthropic is downplaying the incident, saying several sources he considers highly reliable told him Cathedral gained full admin access to the Slack workspace, could read every message, and could log into any user account.
Both the Anthropic and OpenAI labs stored all of their research secrets in Slack, Depue added, with admin API keys scattered across their systems. Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic employee who left the company in September 2026, had previously criticized Anthropic for running dangerous AI research on office software like Slack.
Graham pushed back, saying Depue's sources were wrong. Citing the sensitivity of the matter, he declined to get into specifics but confirmed Depue's core concern: the industry now has to reinvent its security every year.
Depue pressed for details about exactly which claims were false and called on Anthropic to disclose what Cathedral actually accessed. He also blamed the problem on the pace of the AI race, where executives prioritize speed over security.
Alex Stamos, chief security officer at the AI startup Cognition, which uses Anthropic's models, told the Washington Post that he considered the findings significant. He noted that integrated third-party apps are a major problem across the industry and that Anthropic could have done a better job securing its external services.
AI agents are transforming cybersecurity
After months of warnings about AI-powered cyberattacks and its own accidental security incidents, Anthropic is now on the receiving end. AI agents are changing how cyberattacks work, and this breach shows how fast the shift is happening. It's also not just any breach, since Anthropic is likely the company best equipped to defend itself against AI-led attacks.
Graham used the moment to warn that attackers already run AI agents around the clock, specifically targeting external dependencies. Even models half a generation to a full generation behind the current frontier are capable enough for these attacks, he said, and future adversaries will inevitably have more powerful systems at their disposal.
Graham's answer is continuous in-house penetration testing and rebuilding software with formal verification, which AI now makes economically viable. "You probably want to red team yourself all the time. Current models are very creative," Graham wrote.
What he did not address is how Cathedral managed to penetrate this deeply despite Anthropic having access to what are arguably the world's most powerful AI models for cyberdefense.

deep-tech-e1b4cd13aa.headline: India Targets Higher Electronics Value Addition, Semiconductor Packaging and Mature-Node Chips
deep-tech-e1b4cd13aa.fulltext:
Strat360 report identifies components, packaging and customer-qualified production as priorities for India's electronics and semiconductor industry over five years.
India’s electronics industry is expanding, but increasing domestic value addition and building semiconductor manufacturing capabilities remain key challenges, according to a new report from Strat360 Private Limited.
The report, India’s Electronics and Semiconductor Industry: Potential, Recent Developments, Challenges and Policy Priorities, published under the firm’s Strategy-Wise research brand, identifies components, semiconductor packaging and test, and selected mature-node chip manufacturing as priorities for the next five years.
Electronics production reached an estimated INR13.11 lakh crore in fiscal 2026, up 15.8% from INR11.32 lakh crore in FY25, the report said. Exports totalled INR4.24 lakh crore, or about $47.96 billion, making electronics India’s third-largest export category. Mobile phones accounted for the largest share of exports among individual products.
“India has built a world-class assembly base, and its semiconductor journey has begun. The opportunity now is to build depth on that foundation, in components, packaging and mature-node chips. The next five years will reward what customers qualify and reorder, and India is well placed to deliver on that,” said Santosh Tiwari, founding chair of Strat360.
India’s semiconductor manufacturing activity has started with five packaging and test units entering commercial production under the India Semiconductor Mission, according to the report. The Semicon 2.0 programme, approved in July 2026 with an outlay of Rs. 1,27,500 crore, extends government support for the sector.
Domestic component production is another focus. By August 2026, the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) had approved 106 projects, with 38 plants reportedly in production. The report identifies the scheme as a route to increasing domestic value addition in mobile phones from an estimated 18-20% to 35-40%.
The report also identifies opportunities in materials, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, front-end fabrication and the commercialisation of Indian chip designs. India’s first commercial semiconductor fab, planned for Dholera, Gujarat, is expected to begin operations around mid-2028 at mature process nodes.
For the next five years, Strat360 sees the strongest near-term opportunities in packaging and test, components, and selected mature-node and compound-semiconductor production serving automotive, power, industrial and strategic markets. It recommends assessing chip design programmes by commercial outcomes rather than employment or headcount alone.
The report calls for policy support tied to measurable production milestones, including qualified output, yields and domestic value addition. It also recommends regular publication of data on customer qualification, order books and disbursements against actual spending.
Other priorities include sustaining ECMS implementation, setting time limits on subsidies as companies become competitive, and improving access to customers. The report points to Vietnam and Malaysia as examples of countries that have attracted suppliers and customers alongside manufacturing facilities.
“The goal for India is resilience: credible, alternative capacity in assembly, test and components that global customers trust. With milestone-linked policy and a sharp focus on qualified output, India can move from assembly to advantage,” Tiwari said.

global-economics-9374c5c1c9.headline: Fed holds interest rates steady at 3.9% as US inflation remains elevated
global-economics-9374c5c1c9.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News

Updated - October 29, 2026  at 04:17 AM.
| 
         Washington
     The Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Wednesday at about 3.9 per cent despite stubbornly high inflation, while providing little hint about the central bank’s next moves.
“Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting. Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s 2 per cent inflation target, the statement said.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2 per cent target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases.
The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets. Whether the Fed is still leaning toward another hike will likely be a key issue in the news conference held by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh this afternoon.
The Fed’s decision comes just six days before a midterm election that has focused heavily on concerns around the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. Yet Warsh faces plenty of challenges in getting inflation back to target. Some of the forces pushing up prices — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates.
Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday’s decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. This is Cook’s first dissent since she was appointed to the board by President Joe Biden in 2022.
Cook has been targeted by the Trump administration, which tried to fire her last year, though the Supreme Court in June ruled she could keep her job while litigation played out. No president has fired a Fed governor before, a sign of the Fed’s longstanding independence from day-to-day politics. Trump renewed his attempt to remove Cook last month by setting up a committee to look into allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud, which she has denied.
President Trump has also slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank’s rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed.
Other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4 per cent earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans’ sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7 per cent compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4 per cent rate in February, just before the Iran war.
And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3 per cent in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed’s 2 per cent target.
A separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, comes out Thursday and is forecast to have jumped 3.6 per cent in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4 per cent in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1 per cent, up from 3 per cent the previous month.
The Fed’s policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5 per cent. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.
For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the US economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2 per cent, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3 per cent, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2 per cent in the April-June quarter.
Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren’t particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

work-careers-21abac410b.headline: 52% of Indian CEOs plan workforce cuts as AI reshapes hiring: Which jobs are at risk?
work-careers-21abac410b.fulltext:
The report, based on a survey of 125 Indian CEOs conducted between August 11 and September 21, 2026, also found that 87% are focusing on retaining and retraining high-potential employees. Meanwhile, 84% are redesigning roles, career paths and team structures to strengthen collaboration between humans and AI.
Entry-level jobs and routine tasks under scrutiny
The findings point to a shift in workforce planning, with companies seeking employees who can work alongside AI systems while reassessing the skills required for existing and new roles.
However, the report does not identify specific job functions most likely to face reductions. The extent of the impact on entry-level hiring, routine administrative work and other roles will depend on how individual companies deploy AI and reorganise their operations.
The implications for early-career employees could nevertheless be significant. KPMG found that 86% of Indian CEOs are reassessing the skills required for entry-level roles, while 79% said AI is changing how they train and develop employees.

This suggests that employers are reviewing not only the number of workers they need but also the capabilities required to perform jobs in an AI-enabled workplace.
Reskilling becomes a priority
Companies are also investing in training and redeployment as they prepare employees for changing responsibilities. According to the report, 48% of Indian CEOs are prioritising workforce-wide AI education, 44% are providing role-specific training and 41% are retraining employees for AI-supported roles.
Sunit Sinha, Partner and Head of Human Capital Advisory Solutions at KPMG in India, said: “Workforce transformation is no longer simply about preparing people to use new technologies. It is about redesigning roles, building adaptable skills and creating a culture of continuous learning so that people and AI can work together effectively.”
He added that organisations investing in their workforce with the same urgency as their technology investments would be better positioned to translate AI adoption into sustainable value.
ALSO READ: BT BIG STORY: B-school students are increasingly eyeing the start-up route even before their first job
Hiring and job cuts could happen together
The coexistence of workforce reductions and technology hiring suggests that AI-led transformation may change the composition of company workforces rather than simply increase or reduce overall employment.
For employees, the report underscores the importance of developing AI-related capabilities and adapting to changing job requirements. For businesses, the challenge will be to balance productivity gains with talent retention, employee redeployment and the need for specialised skills.
Whether AI ultimately reduces headcount or creates new employment opportunities will depend on how companies implement the technology, redesign workflows and translate productivity improvements into business growth. The KPMG findings reflect CEOs’ current plans and priorities, rather than confirmed future job cuts.

agritech-c1d31901ae.headline: India may import more food, feed and farm commodities as drought hits crops
agritech-c1d31901ae.fulltext:
Cooking oil imports could increase as kharif soybean and groundnut output is expected to fall, while concerns persist over the winter mustard crop. The sugar industry has already secured an extension for raw sugar imports. The poultry industry is seeking permission to import soybean meal and maize, while textile makers want the removal of import duty on cotton. The starch industry fears it may need to import more starch from China if more maize is diverted to ethanol production.
The impact of El Nino on agriculture is set to increase the share of imported staples in Indian kitchens, as the strongest El Nino on record has hit the production of essentials such as pulses, sugar, oilseeds and paddy.
India's soybean imports from the least developed countries in Africa have surged to a record level, as last year's crop was affected by excess rainfall. The soybean shortages are expected to continue in this financial year, as drought has wilted crops across Marathwada, Vidarbha, Telangana, and parts of Madhya Pradesh. "We have requested the government to allow import of 30 lakh tonnes of soybean meal as the prices of soybean meal and maize, which account for 80% of poultry feed, are already high, even as the harvest is going up," said Divya Kumar Gulati, former president, Compound Livestock Feed Manufacturers Association. "If we don't allow imports, then the prices of poultry can go haywire and the farmers will suffer losses." Along with soybean, the production of kharif groundnut could fall more than 20% this year, according to the latest estimate of the Solvent Extractors' Association.
"We expect the overall edible oil imports to increase from 16.5 million tonnes in 2025-26 to 17.5 million tonnes in 2026-27, as we are facing the impact of drought on our domestic oilseeds production. We will have to wait and watch the production of the mustard crops to know the exact figures," said Sandeep Bajoria, CEO of Sunvin Group, a commodity brokerage house.

indian-startups-3d183480cf.headline: AI startup Simplismart raises $14M from Dallas Venture Capital, Nvidia, and others
indian-startups-3d183480cf.fulltext:
Simplismart said it will use the funding to develop its tech platform, for market expansion, and partnerships.
AI inference infrastructure startup Simplismart has raised $14 million in a Series B funding round led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax.
The company will use the funds to further develop its AI inference platform, expand its partnerships with cloud providers and sovereign AI initiatives, and strengthen its presence in North America and other global markets.
Simplismart builds software that connects AI models with GPU infrastructure. Its modular inference engine enables businesses to configure models based on their speed, cost and performance requirements, while its orchestration platform manages deployment and scaling across cloud and on-premises infrastructure.
“We have spent four years building the software layer between the model and the GPU, helping customers optimise how their workloads are deployed and operated. This funding will allow us to take that platform to more enterprises and cloud providers globally,” said Amritanshu Jain, Co-founder and CEO, Simplismart.
The company said its annualised revenue run rate has grown 14-fold over the past six months. It counts companies such as HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema among its customers, which use its platform to run production workloads across video, voice, multimodal and enterprise AI applications.
For its cloud-provider offering, Simplismart works with NVIDIA to deploy AI infrastructure. Unlike inference providers that purchase or reserve GPU capacity and resell it, Simplismart does not own compute infrastructure. Instead, it provides the software layer that enables third-party GPU fleets to run production AI workloads, positioning itself as a data centre enabler.
The platform allows cloud providers to offer managed AI services under their own brands without having to build the underlying software stack from scratch.
“Simplismart is rapidly emerging as a global player helping enterprises run AI workloads more efficiently, while enabling cloud providers to turn GPU capacity into scalable services. We are backing this fast-growing company because of its proven technical prowess in addressing a critical need in the AI infrastructure ecosystem globally, as well as the strong execution capabilities of its founding team,” said Dayakar Puskoor, Managing Partner, Dallas Venture Capital.

ai-2caeea9abb.headline: Google Deepmind releases Gemini 4 Carbon just two weeks after Argon with gains across the board
ai-2caeea9abb.fulltext:
Google Deepmind releases Gemini 4 Carbon just two weeks after Argon with gains across the board
Key Points
- Just two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Carbon, its next frontier model. Carbon tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 with 59 points, up from Argon's 50.
- Google says Carbon is built for multi-day, autonomous development workflows. It's closing the gap fast in Artificial Analysis's Coding Agent Index (59 points vs. Argon's 50) but still trails Claude Opus 5.5 (62 points).
- Because of its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, Carbon is going through the U.S. government's voluntary pre-testing process and will only be available to selected security experts at first. Pricing stays the same as Argon.
Google Deepmind shipped Gemini 4 Carbon just two weeks after Argon, and the new model takes the top spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.
Carbon scores 59 points on the recently updated version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, while predecessor Argon trails at 50. Beyond general gains in agentic tasks and programming, Google highlights capabilities spanning the full cyber defense lifecycle, from detecting and validating vulnerabilities to patching them.
Built for multi-day coding sessions
Google Deepmind says it designed Carbon for "much harder, long-horizon engineering problems" that demand persistent agentic workflows. Internal teams ran the model for multiple days straight, during which it worked through dead ends on its own and handled complex, multi-step tasks like root-cause analysis and subtle bug fixes in large codebases and low-level software, Google claims.
Google also reports improvements in scientific reasoning, multimodal understanding, and full-stack web development based on user feedback. Higher-quality outputs and artifacts in web development pushed Carbon up 89 Elo points on the WebDev Arena, where it sits in fourth place at 1,769.
On Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection benchmark, Carbon pushed the attack success rate from 0.7 percent with Argon down to 0.0 percent, blocking every tested manipulation attempt according to Google. That doesn't mean prompt injection is solved, but the test appears to be saturated.
Independent evaluations back up Google's numbers
According to Artificial Analysis, Carbon at its highest reasoning tier ("high") leads the Intelligence Index v5 mainly because of top scores in complex reasoning, knowledge retrieval, and scientific tasks, taking first place in four of the index's nine individual evaluations.
In agentic coding on Antigravity, Carbon still trails Claude Code with Opus 5.5 by three points, despite jumping from 53 to 59 compared to Argon. In agentic knowledge work on AA-Briefcase, Carbon (high) gains 126 points over Argon (high, 1,483 Elo) to reach 1,609 Elo, driven by presentation quality (+293 Elo to 1,598) and analytical quality (+120 Elo to 1,671). It still falls behind Kimi K3.1 Pro (1,678 Elo), Muse Wonder (max, 1,659 Elo), and Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 1,638 Elo).
Answer accuracy rises from 48 to 58 percent compared to Argon, while the hallucination rate climbs from four to 11 percent. That's higher but still the second-lowest in the ranking. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max) each sit at 50 percent.
The evaluation platform Vals AI puts Carbon in second place at 70.36 percent accuracy, behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (70.85 percent) and ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (70.18 percent) and Argon in fourth (69.24 percent), all at lower cost.
On Vals.ai, Carbon also leads both the Finance Index and the Legal Research benchmark. In legal research, Vals AI recorded roughly 45 percent more cited sources, more frequent tool calls, and longer responses than Argon.
But tasks in the Finance and Tax Agent benchmark take more than twice as long as with Argon, and in Legal Research, Carbon averages more than 50 minutes per task. The model generates 2.3 times as many reasoning tokens and 64 percent more output tokens than Argon, though that's still less than half the output token count of Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5.
On Arena.ai, Gemini 4 Carbon (High) takes the Text Arena lead with 1,528 points, edging past Argon (1,520). On in-house benchmarks, Carbon reportedly produces secure code more than twice as often as Argon, and in tests by Google's Chrome team, it performed more than ten times better at writing security patches than the frontier model of an unnamed competitor.
Security experts get access first

Selected cybersecurity experts get access first starting this week. Through Google Deepmind's Fairwind Program, access will expand to more trusted partners after that.
The company plans to open the model to developers, businesses, and consumers through its product interfaces after collecting more feedback and adjusting the safety guardrails.

Carbon costs $7.76 per task in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, about 23 percent less than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, $10.04) and roughly 1.2 times more than GPT-6 Astra (max, $6.25). ai-077dbdc75a.headline: Anthropic IPO filing warns some risks may be uninsurable. AI coverage will be issue for every company
ai-077dbdc75a.fulltext:
Anthropic's IPO filing includes many words covering many risks, from IP theft to security incidents, data loss, climate change, rogue agents and all the way to an existential crisis for humanity. Embedded in all of the risk language are basic questions about insurance: What's going to be covered? Is it even possible to provide a policy for all of the ways that AI could go wrong? Anthropic, even with more cash than almost any company in America, couldn't answer that question with confidence.
"Because our models may behave in ways that no user or developer intended, claims arising from such actions could result in substantial liability. Our insurance policies also may not provide sufficient coverage to adequately mitigate the potential liabilities we face, especially where any one incident, or a group of incidents, causes disproportionate harm," the company's S-1 filing states. "In addition, with the scale of harm that could result from a catastrophic AI-related incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have sufficient capacity or expertise to underwrite insurance commensurate with such exposure. Further, the insurance market for AI-specific risks is nascent and evolving, and we may be unable to obtain coverage for certain AI-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, leaving us exposed to potentially significant uninsured losses."
Those risks are far removed from AI chatbots helping to book airline tickets or find the best deals on a backyard grill. But there have been increasing instances where AI chatbots are going rogue and some companies are watching warily — even blocking them. In some extreme cases, chatbots are being accused of contributing to a death, including a case revealed this week, raising insurance questions for which there are no easy answers. And with AI starting to permeate seemingly every part of every business ecosystem, the risk of exposure and liability connected to AI continues to increase, and that has the insurance industry on alert.
Alissa Lugo, a senior director analyst in Gartner's legal & compliance practice, says her research shows "death by AI" claims could exceed 2,000 worldwide by end of 2026 — defined as cases in which AI played some role in a fatality, and that number is expected to grow.
Lugo says more companies are building in AI exclusions, and that ultimately insurers, with assistance from the courts, will decide the parameters of AI coverage and how it fits in. Claims for bodily injury, in particular, are where cyber insurance coverage gets thin.
Many experts, including Lugo, compare AI liability today to the early days of cyber insurance.
"Right now, cyber is the policy doing the most to cover AI, but it only covers one kind of AI loss. Cyber responds when AI is involved in a data breach, a privacy violation, a system outage, or a deepfake wire fraud," said Dennis Hendrickson of Hendrickson Insurance, an independent brokerage in Sarasota, Florida.
Hendrickson noted that some cyber carriers have widened their wording to include AI-driven security events. "That's useful. But nearly every cyber policy excludes bodily injury. Cyber was built for data and dollars, not for people getting hurt. This is where there is a major problem, in my opinion," he said, calling the lack of bodily injury or physical damage coverage a "gaping hole" that will need to be addressed.
Gaps in AI insurance coverage
Kara Higginbotham, head of professional liability and cyber for U.S. national accounts at Zurich North America, says AI is creating new exposures across various product lines, but how insurers are navigating it varies greatly by line of business. "Every line of business is handling things a bit differently," she said.
Some companies, including Zurich, have a suite of approved AI tools for workers to use, while others are blocked, and she said safeguards may have to be built into policies as a matter of course for AI protection going forward. But for now, she said, a gap still generally exists in coverage when it comes to bodily harm or physical harm from an AI-related incident.
"It is a gap because it is not being covered by default. A lot of carriers would be wary to write that into a policy today, because as carriers, we have to be able to underwrite risk," Higginbotham said, noting that these are scenarios that are too new and not understood well enough yet, though general liability could in some cases be extended to cover them.
"Insurers are saying, 'We can't cover what you can't show us.' Most companies can't say where their employees are using AI tools. That's the first thing to fix," said Henrietta Akpata, executive fellow and visiting professional lecturer of management and AI at Marist University.
Akpata says this isn't just a problem for big tech companies. A local business whose website chatbot gives a customer the wrong answer, or an HR team using AI to sort job applications, could run into issues. "Those are everyday uses, and they may no longer be covered," Akpata says.
Experts seem divided as to whether AI insurance will evolve into a widespread separate product or be folded into existing cyber policies. Hendrickson says financial-loss AI coverage will become routine and priced like cyber. Bodily injury from AI will be the hard line. Expect tight underwriting, low sub-limits, and requirements for a human to review what the AI does before it reaches a patient. Some healthcare-adjacent businesses won't be able to buy it at all, insurance experts say.
Jaymin Kim, who leads emerging technologies in Marsh's cyber practice, says that so far the firm isn't seeing a ton of AI claims, and she believes that AI issues should be handled within existing insurance policies — including cyber, media, casualty, and first party insurance, among others — though underwriting guidelines and pricing, among other factors, may need to be adjusted. "AI is not a peril. It's just a technology through which existing familiar categories of harms and losses might manifest," said Kim, who noted that trying to separate out AI into its own insurance category could be very tedious.
"We're increasingly seeing AI being embedded in everyday business activities, and so by virtue of that, it's becoming invisible and ubiquitous. Which means on the insurance side, you cannot practically isolate AI in the causal chain of loss," Kim said. She added that just because AI happened to be involved in a data privacy event or a security event, it's still a data privacy or security event. She added that managing competing policies could be a nightmare for a customer.
"Are we saying now we're going to have one CGL policy for everything that doesn't touch AI, and then a second CGL policy for everything that does touch AI?" Kim said.
The industry has not yet seen a wholly new category of risk created by AI, but Kim conceded, "maybe the operative word is 'yet.'"
What cyber insurance history says about the AI risk future
Vikram Desai, global cyber strategy, risk and architecture lead at Accenture, said that until recently, every conversation was about getting AI into the business. "Now, it's about what happens when it goes wrong. That's exposed how badly AI fits the policies companies already own," Desai said.
In some respects, that is similar to the early days of cybersecurity. "Cyber risk sat silently inside general liability for years until insurers named it, excluded it, then sold it back. AI is on the same curve, but compressed," Desai said. "The real exposure is the AI companies don't know they have. Exclusions can bite when AI sits anywhere in the causal chain, including inside a vendor's product," Desai added.
He says underwriters are already asking where AI is being used and who is overseeing it.
Higginbotham said most of the AI-related claims being made today don't involve headline-grabbing, network-shutdown-type attacks, but rather more pedestrian claims around intellectual property — primarily against AI developers accused of scraping content used to train the model, or infringement claims alleging an AI model was trained on copyrighted content. "We also have seen data misuse or privacy-related claims," Higginbotham said.
One complication is that on the cyber side, it isn't always immediately apparent whether AI was used in a social engineering attack — for instance, someone sending an email or Teams message impersonating a colleague.
"We know that bad actors are using AI in more convincing ways to carry out attacks, and that is buoying cyber claims, accelerating them," Higginbotham said, but she added that it isn't always clear what role AI played. "So it will not be a separate category," she said, adding that cyber insurance is designed to handle this kind of exposure.
She says that if the insurer sees "a sustained change in claim development patterns," it may have to start charging more for the coverage if it presents issues for the balance sheet from loss exposure, "but we are not there yet," she added.
"Our underwriting will have to evolve and adapt to changes in the threat environment. We are currently working on partnering with law firms and tech vendors to help," Higginbotham said. "We are not always looking to exclude the next risk — we want to help companies manage risk," she said.
Companies that have not implemented baseline controls may eventually be subject to exclusions if they prove unwilling to change their risk management approach. "But we don't jump to exclusions as the first arrow in the quiver," Higginbotham said.
Hendrickson, like others, is seeing parallels to cyber insurance, and he says he is waiting for the deluge of claims that he is certain is coming, and that he says no one is prepared for, including the large carriers.
"We've seen this before with cyber insurance. First insurers stopped covering it, then they created separate policies for it, and their checklists ended up setting the rules companies followed. I expect the same with AI: for many businesses, insurers will set the standards before the government does," he said.
"Insurance companies come out with a new product, then the claims come in, and they won't renew the policy," Hendrickson said, adding that it's often independent agents like him left bearing the brunt from irate or uncovered customers. "We're the ones in the trenches dealing with this every day."
Correction: Jaymin Kim, who leads emerging technologies in Marsh's cyber practice, believes that AI issues should be handled within existing insurance policies — including cyber, media, casualty, and first party insurance, among others. An earlier version of this article mischaracterized her assessment.

deep-tech-b5aa5b61d7.headline: Indian Army Seeks UAV-Launched Interceptor Drones to Boost Counter-Drone Range and Loiter Time
deep-tech-b5aa5b61d7.fulltext:
As the threat of low-cost, expendable rogue drones continues to disrupt traditional airspace security, the Indian Army is actively conceptualising a shift in its interception tactics.
To bridge the gap in response times, the military is exploring the deployment of kinetic interceptor drones directly from airborne platforms, rather than relying solely on traditional ground-based launches.
Tactical Advantage of Airborne Deployment
In standard counter-UAV operations, ground-launched interceptors face a stark physical limitation: the energy and time required to ascend to the target's altitude significantly drain their battery reserves.
By utilising existing Medium-Altitude Long-Endurance (MALE) and Short-Range UAVs (SR-UAV) as "motherships," the Army aims to position interceptors at optimal altitudes before an engagement even begins.
Releasing an interceptor from a patrolling UAV fundamentally changes the interception geometry. It eliminates the initial climb phase, thereby conserving power.
This conserved energy directly translates to a substantially extended operational range and prolonged loiter time, allowing the interceptor to pursue, track, and neutralise highly manoeuvrable kamikaze drones or loitering munitions with greater efficiency.
Engineering and Industrial Implications
To achieve this capability rapidly, the Army is heavily leaning on India’s private defence sector.
Rather than commissioning a bespoke airborne carrier, the focus remains on retrofitting existing fleets to carry modified versions of vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) interceptors that are currently being designed for ground troops.
This requirement poses a unique engineering challenge for private firms. Drones originally engineered for ground deployment are structurally optimised for static launches, allowing manufacturers to reduce certain complexities and weight.
Transitioning these systems for an aerial release from an aircraft in motion will demand robust design modifications, specialised launcher interfaces, and integrated avionics to ensure safe separation and immediate flight stabilisation mid-air.
Building a Comprehensive Defence Shield
The push for an airborne interceptor mothership is a critical component of a much broader, multi-layered counter-drone architecture being established across the Indian armed forces.
Recognising that no single system can defeat all drone threats, the military is investing across the spectrum.
While the Army advances handheld kinetic drone-killers for immediate tactical defence, the Indian Air Force is concurrently evaluating armed helicopters paired with artificial intelligence to detect and destroy incoming swarms.
Ultimately, this proactive evolution from ground-based to air-launched interception highlights a maturing defence strategy, ensuring that India's armed forces can outpace the rapidly advancing complexities of modern drone warfare.

Huawei Technologies is already integrating elements of the Tau Scaling Law – a new chip design principle that helps the company overcome US export controls – into its wireless communications network, as it pushes for broader adoption across its products.
The Chinese tech giant is using the “time compression” concept based on its Tau Scaling Law in its next-generation wireless base stations, according to a company statement released on Wednesday, and the new design is already delivering tangible gains in performance and efficiency.
The firm’s latest UBBPi baseband products, which integrate the time compression concept, deliver a 1.3-fold increase in average network experience, while cutting energy consumption by 40 per cent, the statement said.
The announcement marks the first application of the Tau Scaling Law in Huawei’s base stations – and another milestone in the company’s breakneck roll-out of the new chip design framework.
In May, Huawei first unveiled its Tau Scaling Law and LogicFolding architecture, key semiconductor breakthroughs aiming to deliver transistor performance equivalent to a 1.4-nanometre process node by 2031 without the need for advanced lithography tools that are inaccessible in China.
The Tau Scaling Law, which focuses on time compression and system-level architectural efficiency rather than shrinking physical chip sizes, is viewed as a strategic engineering response to crippling US export controls on advanced chipmaking equipment.
The latest expansion of the principle into Huawei’s communications network comes after the company already rapidly moved to integrate it across its smartphones and computing infrastructure over the past few months.
In September, the company launched the Kirin 9050 Pro, the first commercial chip employing its LogicFolding architecture. Powering Huawei’s new Mate XT 2 trifold smartphone, the Kirin 9050 Pro delivers a 42 per cent leap in overall performance over its predecessor alongside improved power efficiency, according to the company.
The company also planned to deploy the LogicFolding architecture on its flagship Ascend 990 AI chip around 2030, it said.
The launch of Huawei’s latest telecoms products also comes as Beijing lays the groundwork for the early commercialisation of 6G mobile network technology.
In September, China laid out a road map for building a world-leading next-generation telecommunications network by 2030, as part of a five-year plan issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.
Alongside the UBBPi broadband series, Huawei also launched VitaAAU, which it claimed to be the world’s first commercial Upper 6 GHz equipment. Upper 6 GHz refers to the upper half of the 6 GHz radio frequency spectrum, which serves as a critical bridge for enhancing 5G-Advanced networks and a foundation for future 6G deployment.

Net profit was 39.78 trillion won ($30 billion), while net cash expanded to 98.7 trillion won (~$74 billion).
“SK Hynix’s third-quarter results are very significant in terms of hitting record-high earnings and delivering on shareholder value,” MS Hwang, research director at Counterpoint Research, noted. “First and foremost, operating profit beat expectations again, coming in at 83 trillion won [~$62 billion] versus the consensus of 77 trillion won [~$57 billion].”
According to Counterpoint Research, standard DRAM pricing surged from 20 cents to 30 cents per Gb to $2 per Gb, driving financial momentum and expanding the global DRAM market to $200 billion. “The driving force behind this is rising prices,” Hwang said. “Prices that used to sit around 20 to 30 cents per Gb have now soared to $2.” He also argued that HBM4 will see its unit price jump even further to $4 per Gb.
Additionally, Nvidia resolved initial HBM4 bottlenecks. “Over the past few months, the market has been plagued by two major misconceptions and concerns regarding HBM: That SK was facing technical hurdles in supplying HBM4 to Nvidia, and that HBM adoption volumes per chip might decrease,” he added. “As of October, both concerns have proven to be fake alarms or have been largely resolved.”
As AI expands into enterprise computing, robotics, and autonomous vehicles, SK Hynix projects a structural memory shortage that will persist through 2030. The issue stems from the manufacturing complexity of 10 nm-class, sixth-generation DRAM, and 321-layer NAND.
To secure revenue, SK Hynix said it has signed long-term agreements (LTAs) with 14 tech giants, covering over 50% of capacity for 2027 to 2028. “Today, more than half of the memory industry’s capital expenditure goes into infrastructure,” Hwang said. “This shift in corporate governance leading to stricter capital discipline could ultimately rewrite the traditional memory business cycle.”
SK Hynix said it had discontinued its review of a potential U.S. IPO for its flash memory and solid-state drive subsidiary, Solidigm. “The IPO was intended to raise external capital for the expansion of Solidigm’s production facilities,” SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh Jung said. “However, after carefully considering recent financial market conditions and other factors, we concluded that proceeding at this time would not be the best way to achieve the originally anticipated outcome. We have therefore discontinued our review.”
Hwang commented, “The Solidigm IPO raised issues around a dual listing… If the returns aren’t flowing back to shareholders, it’s very difficult to re-rate the stock.” Additionally, SK Hynix unveiled an expanded fiscal year 2026 shareholder return program of 100 trillion won (~$75 billion), including cash dividends over 30 trillion won (~$22 billion) and buybacks exceeding 60 trillion won (~$45 billion), supported by Kioxia investment gains.
Solidigm is currently in talks with the U.S. Commerce Department to invest $45 billion in a new U.S. chip plant, according to a Bloomberg report citing people familiar with the negotiations. Before committing to what would be the first new major flash-memory chip production facility on American soil, Solidigm is seeking U.S. government permission to send equipment to upgrade an existing plant in Dalian, China.
Counterpoint Research warned of risks such as pullbacks in cloud spending. “The single most severe threat would be a scenario reminiscent of 2018, where cloud service providers simultaneously pull back on their order volume,” Hwang said. “We anticipate that Samsung will surpass SK Hynix from the HBM4 generation, leading the market share in 2027.”
SK Hynix management said it expects to preserve its market lead through proprietary packaging and customer partnerships.

indian-startups-7b6c26b93a.headline: Why Indian AI Founders Are Eyeing Silicon Valley And What They Risk Leaving Behind
indian-startups-7b6c26b93a.fulltext: When AI-powered sales intelligence startup Reo.Dev raised $11.3 Mn in July 2026, its priorities reflected a growing reality for Indian startups building for global markets. The company planned to deploy fresh capital towards expanding sales and marketing operations in the US, which already accounted for nearly two-thirds of its revenue. Yet most of its approximately 75-member workforce remained in India. Reo.Dev is not alone in operating across these two markets. Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based Coreworks AI raised $5 Mn earlier this year to develop its enterprise AI platform. More recently, RapidCanvas secured $29 Mn to expand its go-to-market and field AI engineering teams across India, the US and Brazil. These companies illustrate the increasingly international nature of India's AI startup ecosystem, where the markets founders sell into, the teams they build and the locations from which they operate do not necessarily overlap. The momentum is backed by capital. According to Inc42's Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026, Indian AI startups raised $438 Mn during the July–September quarter, a 265% year-on-year increase. With $676 Mn raised in the first half, cumulative funding for the first nine months of 2026 crossed $1.1 Bn. As more startups pursue global AI opportunities, however, an important question is emerging. Does getting closer to Silicon Valley necessarily make an Indian AI startup more competitive? For Suhas Motwani, cofounder of The Product Folks, a global community of product professionals and builders, the answer is more complicated than a change of address. "The corridor is real, and for a lot of founders it is useful," says Motwani. "The harder question is what gets built on each side of it, and what gets lost when the move happens too early." Why Silicon Valley Is Becoming Harder To Ignore The attraction of Silicon Valley extends well beyond fundraising, which was the case even at the height of the Indian SaaS boom. For AI startups, just like SaaS startups before them, proximity to potential enterprise customers, experienced operators, specialised talent and the wider AI ecosystem can shorten the distance between product development and commercial validation. That matters particularly for startups building enterprise AI products, where customer discovery often requires understanding complex workflows, procurement processes, security requirements and the commercial value of automation. As Inc42 previously explored in its analysis of enterprise AI sales, winning enterprise customers is no longer simply about demonstrating technical capabilities. Startups must identify decision-makers, prove measurable returns and navigate the operational risks associated with deploying AI in live business environments. For companies whose largest potential customers are American enterprises, building those relationships from thousands of kilometres away can introduce additional challenges. Physical presence can create opportunities for more frequent customer interactions, closer feedback loops and a better understanding of how enterprise buying decisions are made. Motwani believes this proximity can be particularly useful in a sector where product capabilities, customer expectations and competitive positioning are evolving rapidly. But there is an important distinction between using Silicon Valley to accelerate learning and treating relocation itself as a competitive advantage. "A low barrier to raising in the Bay is very different from a low barrier to building a durable company," he says. "The move itself is cheap. The compounding effects are not." The challenge for founders is to determine whether their company genuinely needs a physical presence in the US, and what business outcomes that presence is expected to deliver. How AI Is Changing The India–US Equation The India–US technology corridor is not new. Indian SaaS companies have spent years building products and engineering teams at home while selling to enterprise customers abroad. However, AI is changing the economics of that relationship. The cost and complexity of developing frontier AI models continue to demand enormous capital, computing infrastructure and specialised talent. At the same time, access to increasingly capable models is making it possible for smaller teams to build AI-powered applications without developing the underlying technology themselves. The distinction is becoming more visible as the global AI industry enters a new phase. On 26 October, Anthropic publicly filed its registration statement for a proposed US initial public offering. The Claude maker reported approximately $16.3 Bn in revenue during the first half of 2026, compared with about $1.2 Bn in the corresponding period last year, illustrating the rapid commercial expansion of the frontier AI industry. Its proposed listing also comes amid questions over the enormous capital requirements and long-term economics of building advanced AI models. For Indian founders, the implications extend beyond the public market performance of companies such as Anthropic. While frontier AI development remains heavily capital-intensive, application-layer startups can increasingly build on models developed elsewhere, allowing them to direct more resources towards solving specific customer problems. This distinction is particularly relevant to India. According to the Google × Inc42 Bharat AI Startups Report, 2026, 90% of funded Indian AI startups covered in its analysis operate at the application layer. However, access to powerful models also means that technological capabilities can become easier for competing startups to replicate. A sophisticated AI feature, by itself, may no longer constitute a lasting competitive advantage. What becomes harder to replicate is a startup's understanding of its customers, its integration into their workflows, its distribution network and the trust it builds through repeated use. This is where the India–US corridor takes on a different significance. For application-layer startups, being close to Silicon Valley can offer access to frontier AI developments, customers and distribution networks. But the ability to build quickly, experiment cost-effectively and develop products for demanding users can remain rooted in India. The opportunity is no longer just about exporting Indian engineering capabilities to the US. It is about determining which parts of an AI business need to operate closer to the technology frontier, which need to be closer to customers, and where the startup can build its strongest competitive advantage. Knowing The Risks For much of the past decade, Indian technology startups have competed globally by combining engineering talent, leaner operating structures and access to international markets. AI is changing the economics of building software, but it has not eliminated the importance of these advantages. Moving an entire founding or engineering team to San Francisco can significantly increase operating costs, particularly when the startup is still experimenting with products, pricing and its target customer segment. More importantly, an early relocation can affect the company's product development process. Founders who move away from their engineering teams may find themselves managing critical product decisions across time zones. The resulting separation can make experimentation, communication and decision-making more complex at precisely the stage when startups need to move quickly. There is also the question of which users influence the product roadmap. A startup developing AI products for American enterprises may benefit enormously from spending more time with US customers. But the same approach could prove counterproductive for a company building for Indian consumers, small businesses or enterprises with distinctly local requirements. Motwani argues that the environment in which a startup develops its earliest products can influence the capabilities it prioritises and the problems it learns to solve. India, for instance, exposes AI products to considerable variation in languages, devices, connectivity, user behaviour and willingness to pay. A product designed around affluent, English-speaking users with reliable connectivity may not necessarily work as effectively for consumers using regional languages, shared devices or less predictable networks. These constraints can force teams to improve reliability, usability and cost efficiency much earlier in the product development cycle. The risk is not that an Indian founder builds for the US. It is that the founder changes markets without deliberately reassessing which customers, capabilities and advantages should shape the business. An Opportunity Too Large To Overlook The case for maintaining a strong presence in India is also increasingly supported by the size of the domestic opportunity. According to the Google × Inc42 Bharat AI Startups Report, 2026, India's AI market is projected to reach $126 Bn by 2030. Enterprise AI expenditure is estimated to grow from $11 Bn in 2025 to $71 Bn by 2030, while consumer AI expenditure is projected to rise from $13 Bn to $55 Bn over the same period. For application-layer startups, this represents a significant opportunity to build products that address specific customer problems, integrate into existing workflows and earn sustained adoption. There are, however, important differences between market opportunity and commercial readiness. India was already the world's second-largest market for AI application downloads in 2024, accounting for 177 Mn downloads. Yet the Bharat AI report estimated consumer AI monetisation at just $12 Mn during that period. In other words, significant user adoption does not automatically translate into strong monetisation. For Indian AI founders, this creates two different opportunities. The US offers access to enterprise customers with established software budgets, while India offers a large and diverse market in which startups can build products around local workflows and underserved customer segments. Choosing between them should depend on the problem being solved, rather than the assumption that one market is inherently superior. There are also alternative routes to global customers that do not require startups to abandon their Indian operating base. An earlier analysis published on Inc42 examined how India's Global Capability Centres (GCCs) could become an important route to multinational enterprise buyers, offering Indian AI startups access to global workflows and potential decision-makers within the country itself. The major implication is that access to international customers does not always require shifting the entire centre of product development overseas. The Case For Building Across Two Markets Rather than viewing Bengaluru and Silicon Valley as competing destinations, Motwani sees merit in founders using the two ecosystems for different purposes. Through his work with The Product Folks, he has observed differences in the priorities that dominate conversations among founders and product professionals in the two markets. In San Francisco or the Valley, discussions tend to centre on distribution, pricing and category creation. In Bengaluru, they are often more focused on engineering teams, product positioning, capital efficiency and the immediate challenges of building a sustainable business. Both perspectives matter. A startup can build a technically capable AI product in India and still struggle to reach the right international customers. Equally, access to American buyers and investors does not guarantee that the company will develop a defensible product or sustainable business model. This is where a two-market operating strategy becomes relevant. Naukri has developed an AI and data strategy, 99acres has strengthened its market position and become a cash-generating business, while Jeevansathi and Aisle have turned profitable. Oberoi added that he remained financially and emotionally attached to Info Edge and would continue on its board, subject to shareholder approval, despite stepping away from his full-time operating role. other-interests-94a9194559.headline: OpenAI just scooped human researchers on a million-dollar quantum math problem
other-interests-94a9194559.fulltext:
If you’ve been keeping up with news in the math world, the story will sound strikingly familiar, right down to its cast of characters.
Using a proprietary internal large language model (LLM), OpenAI just released a result mathematicians have been chasing for decades: a formal proof validating the “quantum chromodynamics” that underpin physicists’ best, most successful description of the universe.
The new proof also scoops the work of two human mathematicians, one of whom just happens to be employed by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic. The duo—Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge and Ethan Sussman, a mathematician at Northwestern University—had publicly disclosed their progress on their own independent proof in the weeks leading up to OpenAI’s historic announcement.

“I’m not going to say that I’m not disappointed,” Sussman says. He and Alpöge first revealed their burgeoning collaboration to the world on October 6. Notably, the pair updated their public GitHub repository with a new set of intermediate results the night before OpenAI’s announcement. “I think we were on the way and maybe even as close as a few weeks away,” Sussman says.
“This is a major advance,” says Michael R. Douglas, a theoretical physicist and artificial intelligence proponent at Harvard University. “Mathematicians have been trying to make quantum field theory rigorous for over 50 years and have made steady progress, but real-world theories like quantum chromodynamics always seemed out of reach—until now. This is just the start..., but we can hope for rapid progress.”
Both camps were pursuing something known as the Yang-Mills problem, which concerns the math that underpins modern physics. The “Standard Model” of particle physics explains all the known forces in the universe with 17 interacting particles. The particles are described by “quantum fields,” mathematical entities that permeate all of space and time, determining how, when and where particles appear in the world, what they are and what they do.
But the math of quantum fields is notoriously gnarly. Physicists use it to reliably predict what happens when they smash particles together at places such as the Large Hadron Collider, but mathematicians worry that the theory has holes.
The Yang-Mills problem is about putting that theory on a solid mathematical footing. The problem has two parts: proving that the theory is mathematically consistent—that it “exists”—and proving that it has a nonzero quantity called a “mass gap,” which has important consequences in the physical world.
In the 1980s mathematician Tadeusz Balaban laid out a coarse path to proving the first part, “existence.” But even just this bare mathematical sketch of a proof was an enormous undertaking, encompassing thousands of pages. And it was far from complete.
“[Balaban’s] papers are not complete and are extraordinarily difficult to read, but experts did not seriously doubt that they could be completed with sufficiently many years devoted to it,” says Roland Bauerschmidt, a mathematician at New York University.
Even so, decades have passed, and no other expert has managed to reach the top of the mountain Balaban built—let alone bridge the gaps he left along the way. Balaban himself eventually tired of the project and moved on.
Hopes for progress ramped up only this summer as the rapidly accelerating capabilities of LLMs catapulted them to the forefront of research-level math. In particular, the superhuman endurance of LLMs has let them blast through numerical tedium to persevere where any human would lose interest and give up. Suddenly, an exhausted mathematician could carefully prompt an LLM, get a good night’s sleep and then wake up in the morning to find a completed proof from the tireless, dutiful model.
Seeing this, Sussman became convinced LLMs were the perfect tool to work on Balaban’s program. “The primary obstacle was the amount of work involved rather than the absence of ideas,” he says. “So from my perspective, this was a rather obvious thing to do.”
At the same time, Alpöge was producing a number of high-profile results with Anthropic’s Claude family of models. In particular, his wrangling of six-dimensional spheres caught Sussman’s attention. “It was the first instance that I had seen of someone being able to get an LLM to produce, reliably, a 100-page proof,” he recalls. That’s the sort of feat that begins to approach the gargantuan tomes typical of Yang-Mills-related work.
So on September 8—which happened to be one of the biggest days in math history—Sussman e-mailed Alpöge. “I essentially told him, ‘Hey, in case no one else has told you, here is something I think would be worth doing,’” he says. Alpöge invited him to collaborate.
The partnership proceeded much like Alpöge’s work with another mathematician, New York University’s Tristan Buckmaster, on the Euler equations (an important precursor to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, which OpenAI announced it had solved on September 8). Alpöge would use Anthropic’s internal version of Claude—in fact, many “agent” copies of the LLM working in concert—to churn out thousands of pages of mathematical arcana, essentially unreadable to a human. But he’d then use his agents to validate that the arcana corresponded to some real mathematical truth—and to distill it into something easier to parse. He’d then send it to Sussman—who was flabbergasted by how much was borne out by the LLM’s churn.
“It’s remarkable,” Sussman says. “The vast majority, if not all, of the mistakes in the version we posted on GitHub were produced by me.”
In addition to filling in Balaban’s gaps with a tedious litany of mathematical steps, the agents also made some genuine innovations. “I could tell you exactly how it built on older work,” Sussman says of one example, “but it also was somewhat novel.”
On October 6 Sussman and Alpöge heard the rumors that OpenAI was about to release hundreds of major math results and thought Yang-Mills might be one of them. They decided to proactively start staking their own claim by posting their progress in a public GitHub repository. “I certainly was not the only person to realize this was something worth pursuing,” Sussman says. Their revelation quickly made the rounds on X. Then, when OpenAI’s ensuing “slop drop” didn’t contain a Yang-Mills proof, they continued their work in the open, for all to see.
After making significant progress this past weekend, the pair updated their repository on Sunday evening. They believed they’d solved the three-dimensional version of the “existence problem.” This would have fallen short of the Clay Mathematical Institute’s Millennium Prize Problem criteria, which demand a four-dimensional solution, but “we expect, based on the ‘slop’ that we have, that the key ideas are the same,” Sussman says.
On Monday evening OpenAI claimed a proof of the “existence” part of the Clay problem. The company has yet to release the proof; instead OpenAI opted to hand it off to a group of experts who could “shepherd” it into the mathematical literature. This decision sparked immediate outcry, including from the advisory group of mathematicians the company itself had assembled in response to earlier backlash.
Writing on X, Alpöge expressed a mix of disgust and dismay. “I kept telling [Sussman] to not be too deferential and modest because he would be publicly scooped at any opportunity,” Alpöge wrote. “Instead of contacting him to work with him, as has been suggested publicly many times, the people at OpenAI chose to do this.”
In a blog post, OpenAI stated that its internal model—the same one responsible for the Navier-Stokes proof and the subsequent “slop drop”—arrived at the result on September 9. But according to the post, OpenAI opted to keep it secret until the company could code it into Lean, a programming language that helps ensure mathematical correctness. Notably, the OpenAI said this Lean verification took well more than a month, whereas similar checking only took a reported 17 hours for its Navier-Stokes proof.
“There is no way it took one month to Lean-verify Yang-Mills,” says Buckmaster, whose very public bout with OpenAI over Navier-Stokes remains largely unresolved. “It takes, at most, a couple of days.”
As in the Navier-Stokes controversy, this sequence of events shows how impenetrable the provenance of mathematical ideas is becoming. The ongoing rat race between AI companies jockeying for trillion-dollar initial public offering (IPO) valuations continues to come at the cost of scientific clarity and adherence to academic norms. Everyone involved agrees that new norms need to be discussed and established, but no one seems willing to hold back the deluge while that happens.
