KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia (AP) — Malaysia’s customs department said Wednesday it had seized 30 servers equipped with advanced artificial intelligence chips in a suspected export-control violation. Officials believe a syndicate is using Malaysia as a transit hub to re-export the chips to another Asian country.
Malaysia introduced permit requirements for the export, transit and transshipment of high-performance AI chips of U.S. origin last year, under pressure from the U.S. to ensure sensitive technology isn’t rerouted to China through third countries. Washington has sought to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors to curb Beijing’s AI and military capabilities.
The shipment, worth about 50 million ringgit ($12.2 million), was intercepted at the free trade zone area at the country’s main airport during an inspection on Oct. 15, the airport’s customs director Aspalila Ag Tuah told reporters.
The servers, which came from an Asian country, were falsely declared as electric components to avoid detection before being reexported to another Asian country without the required permit, she said.
“The syndicate is using Malaysia as a transit destination to ensure there would be no restrictions imposed while the servers are exported to the next destination,” the customs department said in a statement.
Aspalila said the shipment was believed to be linked to a syndicate behind five attempted smuggling operations, including one in June when customs authorities seized 72 servers containing advanced AI chips at the airport’s free trade zone.
She said a Malaysian firm that facilitated the shipment has been called in to assist investigations. She declined to give further details on the origin of the chips or their final destination, saying the case was under investigation.

This story was originally published on BioPharma Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily BioPharma Dive newsletter.
Dive Brief:
- Eli Lilly's triple-acting metabolic drug retatrutide bested Novo's Ozempic in a head-to-head Phase 3 trial, with the highest dose tested beating Novo's drug on measures of blood sugar and weight loss, the company said Wednesday.
- After 80 weeks of treatment, a 12 milligram weekly dose of retatrutide lowered blood sugar by an average of 2.2 percentage points, significantly more than Ozempic's 1.8 percentage points, Lilly said. A 9 mg dose of retatrutide also lowered blood sugar by 2.2 percentage points, but the difference when compared to Ozempic was statistically "nominal," the company said.
- The results confirm earlier findings suggesting retatrutide — which acts on three metabolic pathways versus one for Ozempic — could be a differentiated diabetes and weight loss medicine. In an obesity trial, this "triple-G" drug stimulated weight loss that rivaled results seen in bariatric surgery.
Dive Insight:
Should retatrutide go on to win approval, Lilly may further cement its place atop metabolic medicine. The ascent of its already-marketed Zepbound and Mounjaro have propelled Lilly's market value far beyond that of its pharmaceutical peers. And the buzz surrounding retatrutide is so strong that many people have resorted to a nebulous "black market" to get their hands on it.
Retatrutide represents the next step in a push by obesity drug developers to make therapies that can drop weight even more profoundly than existing medications. While GLP-1 medicines have been on the market for more than 20 years, for instance — Lilly was the commercial partner for the first such shot — the company has been specializing in drugs that add more metabolic targets to boost effectiveness.
Zepbound and Mounjaro modulate GLP-1 as well as a second hormone called GIP. Retatrutide acts on a third, called glucagon, too. Novo is aiming to catch up, but has yet to launch a dual acting drug, and its three-pronged candidates are in Phase 2 trials.
The latest trial result showed just how challenging a foe retatrutide might be for Novo. The highest dose lowered weight by 21% on average, while a 9 mg dose was associated with 20% weight loss. That number was 9% for Ozempic recipients.
Those benefits appear to come with a trade-off. In the study, only 3% of Ozempic recipients stopped treatment because of side effects compared with 8% of the people on the highest retatrutide dose and 5% of those in the 9 mg group.

NEW DELHI – The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounted to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups told the Supreme Court on Oct 27, starting the most high-profile challenge against the legislation.
The lawsuit comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Prime Minister Narendra Modi took office in 2014. Critics say many mainstream media outlets have not done enough to scrutinise Modi’s government, which has denied such allegations and says it respects press freedom.
A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged the privacy law, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow New Delhi to identify journalists’ sources, Reuters reported on Oct 26.
“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), told the judges. “Newsrooms will shut down if we have to ask for permission... It’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”
The lawsuit is the most high-profile challenge to Modi’s privacy law. Until now, only free speech activists and a group of smaller news outlets had challenged it.
The Supreme Court posted the case for November.
Big media groups v Modi
Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier in October.
The publishers are demanding that most of the law’s contentious provisions, which kick in from May 2027, should be quashed. They say the law could also force publishers to erase stories and give powers to the government to demand information from publishers that could expose reporters’ sources.
DNPA, the group which has challenged Modi’s government, counts as members Ambani’s Network18, Adani’s NDTV and other marquee media groups, including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.
Divan said during the hearing that earlier versions of the law excluded journalists, but the final one did not. REUTERS

global-economics-48b48c80e9.headline: Exclusive-US DOJ is inquiring about Nvidias purchase of Hugging Face, sources say
global-economics-48b48c80e9.fulltext:
ReutersPublished29 Oct 2026, 12:04 AM IST
By Max A. Cherney, Jeffrey Dastin and Jody Godoy
SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The US Department of Justice has made inquiries about how Nvidia’s $12.93 billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face would affect competition in artificial intelligence, at the same time as antitrust enforcers pursue their years-long investigation into the chip designer's conduct, two people familiar with the matter said.
The Justice Department's recent questioning covers Nvidia's acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether the chip designer has exerted pressure on its customers, the two people said. On Hugging Face, Justice Department officials have asked whether the deal would let Nvidia capture a fundamental distribution point for AI, the people said. The acquisition is expected to close in the first half of 2027, Nvidia has said, adding that Hugging Face would continue to support work with a range of chip, cloud and AI providers.
The department's questions around the Hugging Face deal and details of its continued pursuit of Nvidia's conduct more broadly are reported for the first time here. Nvidia has become a cornerstone of the tech economy and AI boom, backing major players such as Anthropic and OpenAI while spurring data center development globally so its chips can power AI's voracious computing needs.
Any action by the DOJ could ripple through the chip industry and challenge Nvidia's investing and acquisition strategy that has extended its influence in AI. Government investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and do not necessarily result in lawsuits.
A DOJ spokesperson declined to comment on any matters before the department, citing longstanding policy. The spokesperson added, "This DOJ under President Trump’s leadership will continue to prioritize advancement of Super Intelligence for the betterment of the American people."
Nvidia declined to comment, and Hugging Face representatives did not respond to a request for comment.
The broad Nvidia examination started under former Democratic President Joe Biden and has continued under the administration of Republican President Donald Trump, during which time Nvidia has been the most valuable company in the world and a singular force in AI. There is no indication that Trump has any involvement, and the probe may not result in any Justice Department action.
As part of the probe, the DOJ has examined Nvidia’s acquisition of SchedMD, one of the people said. The December 2025 purchase sparked worries among AI specialists about their access to SchedMD's open-source software, which helps run supercomputers relevant to national security. Nvidia has vowed to continue open access and support.
NVIDIA AND TRUMP
Nvidia has the biggest share of the market for AI chips, which power the likes of ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and similar tools. A host of startups and chip-design companies have challenged its dominance.
Competitors Broadcom and Alphabet's Google design processors together, seeking to beat Nvidia hardware with chips purpose-built for specific tasks and AI software. Advanced Micro Devices has said it can produce technically superior hardware and has struck billion-dollar deals with several AI labs and cloud computing operators.
Nvidia's market position has nonetheless made it an industry force and helped CEO Jensen Huang develop a relationship with Trump, who has touted American AI. Huang and Trump have made frequent appearances together, with the CEO joining the president's diplomatic trip to China. Trump, who has disclosed owning Nvidia stock, separately awarded Huang the National Medal of Science for advancing AI hardware.
Trump critics have previously accused the administration of political intervention at the DOJ, which the administration has disputed. Such intervention is traditionally out of the ordinary.
Staff-led investigations at the DOJ often take years and can stretch from one administration to the next. In addition, the DOJ routinely seeks input from companies when evaluating proposed mergers. "It would be inappropriate for the Department to conduct a merger investigation under the guise of a conduct investigation," the DOJ spokesperson said.
SCRUTINY OF OTHER NVIDIA DEALS
The DOJ has scrutinized Nvidia's conduct following other transactions, including its 2025 deal to license technology from chip startup Groq and hire its engineers, the people said. Officials have explored whether Nvidia unfairly offered larger allocations of AI chips if customers purchased its networking equipment and Groq processors, raising questions about whether Nvidia used its dominant product to push into a newer market, the people said.
Nvidia declined to comment, and Groq did not respond to a request for comment.
The DOJ has also looked at Nvidia's acquisition of Run:ai, which makes software that helps AI chips run more efficiently, the people said.
The department's questions about the proposed Hugging Face acquisition include identifying how Nvidia might use the AI platform to harm rivals in the AI market, and whether Nvidia could use the newly acquired business to gain leverage, the people said.
Officials are also asking questions about Hugging Face's competitors, said the people.
(Reporting by Max A. Cherney and Jeffrey Dastin in San Francisco and Jody Godoy in New York; Editing by Peter Henderson, David Gaffen and Matthew Lewis)

global-economics-04b35fb562.headline: Fed holds main interest rate steady despite accelerating inflation
global-economics-04b35fb562.fulltext:
Dive Brief:
- The Federal Reserve on Wednesday held the benchmark interest rate steady despite data showing that inflation last month accelerated further beyond the central bank’s 2% goal.
- Policymakers in a 10-2 vote decided to collect more data before considering whether to follow up their quarter-point tightening in September with a second increase in the federal funds rate, the Federal Open Market Committee said in a statement while pledging to “deliver price stability.” Its next scheduled meeting is Dec. 8-9.
- “Inflation remains elevated,” the FOMC said, adding that “the accumulation of more information will help the committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2% goal.” Two policymakers, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of raising the main rate by 0.25 percentage point.
Dive Insight:
Hammack and other policymakers in recent months have voiced concern that inflation will speed up and prove more difficult to curb without a timely increase in borrowing costs.
Indeed, central bank officials during their two-day gathering engaged in a heated discussion about inflation, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in a post-meeting press conference.
“We just came out of a heck of a family fight — serious, sober discussion,” he said.
Policymakers met after data on consumer and wholesale prices in September showed inflation speeding up and prolonging its more than five-year period above the Fed’s target.
The consumer price index rose at a 3.7% annual rate in September, higher than expected. The 12-month gain in the producer price index of 6.3% last month also exceeded forecasts.
Higher energy prices, pushed up by the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, have spurred price increases across much of the economy and show no sign of declining. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil has surged 80% during the past year to $115.75.
The extended period of rising prices has eroded real incomes and undermined household budgets, influencing the outlook of voters with the approach of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
“It’s our responsibility to get inflation down,” Warsh said.
Bond traders since late September have done some tightening for the Fed, pushing up the yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note above 5%.
“Since our policy action in September we have started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions," Warsh said.
“Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations and, while overall financial conditions are tighter, I’m unwilling and unable to call them tight,” he said.
Warsh and the FOMC painted a bright picture of the economy.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the committee said. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.
“Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust,” the FOMC said. “Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”
The job market is healthy, Warsh said. Unemployment was 4.2% in September and has ranged between 4.1% and 4.3% since March, giving the FOMC no apparent reason for forgoing a rate increase.
“On the employment side of the Fed’s dual mandate, conditions are quite positive,” Warsh said. “The jobless rate is lower than a year ago and payroll growth is noticeably above last year’s pace.”
Traders in interest rate futures on Wednesday increased the odds that policymakers will raise the main interest rate by a quarter point in December to 85% from 75% on Tuesday, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. The federal funds rate is currently set at a range from 3.75% to 4%.
Since taking the top post at the central bank in May, Warsh has repeatedly vowed to quell inflation, saying that “inflation is a choice.”
For now, though, with the elections less than a week away, the watchword among policymakers on the topic of inflation is apparently “wait and see.”
“Politics had no role in the decision,” Warsh said, referring to the FOMC vote. “I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs — I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
Editor's note: Story was updated to include comments from the press conference.

global-economics-35992e7760.headline: Fed holds interest rates steady even as inflation remains stubborn
global-economics-35992e7760.fulltext:
Fed holds interest rates steady even as inflation remains stubborn
The Federal Reserve opted not to raise interest rates Wednesday, but signaled that it's not retreating from the fight against stubborn inflation.
The central bank renewed its pledge to deliver price stability, a goal that's been made more difficult by a spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran.
"Inflation remains elevated," the Fed's rate-setting committee acknowledged in a statement.
At its last policy meeting in September, the Fed raised rates for the first time in more than three years. Since then, data has shown inflation has continued to accelerate, with consumer prices in September up 3.7% from a year ago — a bigger annual increase than the previous month.
"It's 'wrong way," says Dan North, a senior economist at the insurance company Allianz Trade. "That inflation line is going up, not down."
The decision not to adjust interest rates comes less than a week before votes are tallied in the midterm election, which may have contributed to the Fed's caution.
"It would be suspicious if there were a hike before the midterm," North said.
Loading...
A December hike is looking likely
After a pause at this week's meeting, Fed policymakers are widely expected to raise their benchmark interest rate at their next meeting in December, in an effort to tamp down demand and bring prices under control.
Two members of the rate-setting committee wanted to move more quickly. Fed governor Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack of the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank voted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point on Wednesday, while a majority of Fed policymakers opted to stand pat.
The Federal Reserve's benchmark rate — currently 3.75 to 4% — helps to establish the cost of other short-term lending for things like credit cards.
Longer-term interest rates are set by the bond market but can also be influenced by Fed decisions. Mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, before easing slightly. The high cost of home loans has been a drag on the housing market, which has been in a slump for the last four years.
AI helps prop up the economy
Other parts of the economy are less sensitive to rising interest rates. The booming investment in artificial intelligence, for example, shows no sign of slowing down, no matter how much the Fed tries to tap on the brakes.
"The A.I. companies don't care what interest rate they have to pay," North says.
The frenzied push to build A.I. data centers is pushing up prices for construction materials and electronic equipment.
Consumer spending has also remained resilient, fueled in part by upper-income shoppers who benefit from the rising stock market.
That's not the case for less wealthy families, whose wages are not keeping pace with the rising cost of living. Average wages rose just 3% for the 12 months ending in September.
"Lower and middle-income Americans are having a real struggle," says Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. " Their purchasing power is actually declining. And that's a pretty uncomfortable place to be. And that likely goes to explain to a large degree why people don't feel very good about the economy."

global-economics-6a84a1a3f6.headline: Fed holds interest rates steady at 3.9% as US inflation remains elevated
global-economics-6a84a1a3f6.fulltext:
Updated - October 29, 2026  at 04:17 AM.
| 
         Washington
     The Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Wednesday at about 3.9 per cent despite stubbornly high inflation, while providing little hint about the central bank’s next moves.
“Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting. Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s 2 per cent inflation target, the statement said.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2 per cent target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases.
The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets. Whether the Fed is still leaning toward another hike will likely be a key issue in the news conference held by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh this afternoon.
The Fed’s decision comes just six days before a midterm election that has focused heavily on concerns around the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. Yet Warsh faces plenty of challenges in getting inflation back to target. Some of the forces pushing up prices — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates.
Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday’s decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. This is Cook’s first dissent since she was appointed to the board by President Joe Biden in 2022.
Cook has been targeted by the Trump administration, which tried to fire her last year, though the Supreme Court in June ruled she could keep her job while litigation played out. No president has fired a Fed governor before, a sign of the Fed’s longstanding independence from day-to-day politics. Trump renewed his attempt to remove Cook last month by setting up a committee to look into allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud, which she has denied.
President Trump has also slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank’s rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed.
Other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4 per cent earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans’ sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7 per cent compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4 per cent rate in February, just before the Iran war.
And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3 per cent in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed’s 2 per cent target.
A separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, comes out Thursday and is forecast to have jumped 3.6 per cent in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4 per cent in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1 per cent, up from 3 per cent the previous month.
The Fed’s policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5 per cent. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.
For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the US economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2 per cent, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3 per cent, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2 per cent in the April-June quarter.
Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren’t particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

global-economics-9c26d66f1b.headline: Fed Meeting Live Updates: Interest Rates Hold Steady Despite 'Elevated' Inflation
global-economics-9c26d66f1b.fulltext:
Fed Holds Rates Steady Despite ‘Elevated’ Inflation
Kevin Warsh, the Federal Reserve chairman, gave an upbeat assessment of the economy but stressed that inflation was too high. He said the Fed would hold fewer rate-setting votes starting next year.
Federal Funds target rate
Latest
- The Federal Reserve held rates steady on Wednesday as expected. The two dissenting officials in favor of a quarter-point increase included Lisa D. Cook, a governor who is fighting to keep her job amid President Trump’s campaign to fire her. Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed’s chairman, leaned into the idea that the central bank had the flexibility to accumulate more information to make the right determination about rates because expectations about future inflation do not point to a lack of confidence in the Fed’s ability to eventually achieve the 2 percent target and because there are no signs the economy is overheating.
- Mr. Warsh’s biggest announcement of the day pertained to how often the Fed will vote on interest rates in the coming years, an idea that The New York Times first reported the chairman raised in July. In 2027, the Fed plans to hold seven policy meetings, with one dedicated to discussing “broad monetary policy strategy.” In 2028, there will be six policy meetings and two on strategy.
- Mr. Warsh repeatedly mentioned a shift in financial conditions since September, which he suggested helped the Fed in the pursuit of its inflation goal on the margins. Credit conditions have “tightened for some businesses and households, much as we would expect,” he said. “Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations, and while overall financial conditions are tighter, I’m unwilling and unable to call them tight. But broadly, these developments go in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.”
- The Fed’s meeting is days before the midterm elections, but Mr. Warsh emphasized that politics played no role in Wednesday’s decision to hold rates steady. But the political backdrop has been hard to ignore, especially because of Mr. Trump’s repeated attacks on the Fed for not complying with his demands for lower rates. The White House has demanded that Ms. Cook attend an in-person hearing to defend herself against allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, something Mr. Trump has cited as a reason to fire her.
The S&P 500 ended the day 0.3 percent higher, after a volatile period of trading while Warsh was speaking. Easier monetary policy, with rates expectations falling, is usually bullish for the stock market.
Starting next year, the Federal Reserve will reduce the number of meetings at which it sets interest rates, Kevin M. Warsh, the central bank’s chairman, announced Wednesday.
The Fed’s 12-member policy committee currently holds eight regularly scheduled meetings a year, a cadence it has maintained since the 1980s. Mr. Warsh, who took over as the Fed’s leader in May, raised the idea of reducing the number of meetings at the committee’s closed-door session in July, a discussion first reported by The New York Times and later confirmed in the publicly released minutes of the meeting.
In a news conference on Wednesday, Mr. Warsh said the Fed would meet eight times next year as usual. But only seven of those meetings will include a vote on interest rates. The eighth “will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy,” he said.
In 2028, the Fed expects to hold just six rate-setting meetings, with two meetings dedicated to discussions of longer-run strategy, Mr. Warsh said.
“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information rich intervals,” Mr. Warsh said, “but it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons.”
Some economists have criticized the idea of holding fewer meetings, arguing it could make it harder for the Fed to respond quickly to changes in inflation and the labor market. The move also fits a pattern during the early months of Mr. Warsh’s chairmanship toward providing less information to investors and the public, reversing a decades-long trend toward greater openness.
Other economists, however, have defended the idea. They argue that providing more time between meetings will make it easier for policymakers to identify meaningful shifts in economic conditions. And they note that the Fed can hold emergency meetings if necessary, as it has done numerous times in the past.
Recent Fed dissents over rates
Investor expectations for interest rate increases have also fallen, further pointing to doubt about the Fed’s resolve to keep raising rates. Robert Dishner, a senior portfolio manager at Neuberger, said that while a December rate increase remains on the table, “the 2027 hikes that the market has priced in may require further consideration.”
There is an interesting dynamic in the market as investors digest Warsh’s comments. The short-dated, two-year Treasury yield has fallen to 4.71 percent, while the 10-year Treasury yield has risen to 5.04 percent. The move in the 10-year was driven by a rise in the breakeven inflation rate, which is a market measure of investors’ inflation expectations. “That to me is literally the market saying that you talk tough on inflation but you are not delivering on it,” said George Goncalves, head of U.S. macro strategy at MUFG Securities.
The biggest question coming into the news conference was why the Fed didn’t raise rates given the persistence of inflation. I’m not sure we ever got an answer, despite the best efforts of reporters to pin Warsh down.
That’s a wrap. Takeaways are coming soon.
Asked if the Fed would participate in a White House hearing on Lisa Cook, which could result in her firing, Warsh simply replied: “Not to my knowledge.”
Warsh says the economy is strong, but not necessarily too hot in a way that is leading to inflation. “Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy too strong? That isn’t the judgment of most of my colleagues,” he says. He argues that productivity growth is picking up, which allows the economy to grow faster without causing inflation.
Warsh reiterated his comments that he “does not believe” in forward guidance. However, he was careful to include a caveat for when the economy is in crisis. Recalling his experience during the 2008 financial crisis, he said that in those moments, guidance is needed.
Warsh is asked about the role that the A.I. investment boom is playing in driving both inflation and economic growth. He says that A.I. is an important factor in the strong economy, but not the only one. And he pushes back against the idea that A.I. investments are insensitive to interest rates, noting that corporate bond investors appear to be distinguishing between A.I. companies that they view as safe and those that could be riskier. In other words, he still believes interest rates will do the job of bringing inflation under control.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” Warsh said when asked about the midterms, which are just days away.
Warsh says that while surveys show that consumers are expecting faster inflation in the near-term, there is relatively little evidence that they are expecting faster inflation over the longer run. That’s generally true, but there have been some hints that consumers are expecting inflation to be higher in the future as well. Economists and policymakers pay close attention to such measures of expectations because if consumers and businesses start to expect inflation to endure, it can make it harder for the Fed to bring it under control.
Warsh is asked about the task forces that he convened to look at a wide range of issues that he believes are central to how the Fed conducts policy. They include groups looking at how the Fed communicates as well as how it models inflation. He said “some, but not all” groups will have recommendations by year-end, the deadline that Warsh initially set.
Reducing the number of meetings is the most major change that Warsh so far has announced at the central bank. The reason that Warsh most often cites is that it will allow for more data to accumulate between votes on interest rates. One potential risk is that it might leave the Fed less nimble to act if the economic backdrop rapidly changes. The Fed can hold emergency meetings, but they only tend to do that during periods of crisis.
Yields have come back down to 5 percent where they started the day. It appeared investors were responding to Warsh’s comments on inflation expectations remaining anchored, despite hotter inflation data in recent weeks. It’s obviously hard to know the precise driver but what is clear is that markets are twitchy, moving quickly higher and lower since Warsh started speaking.
Warsh says the committee is “going to be able to figure out what’s the appropriate protocol” and that he is “encouraged by the progress we’ve made in a short period of time.”
It isn’t clear what progress the Fed has made, given the hot September inflation readings. But he highlights the continued stability of inflation expectations, which he said indicates confidence that the Fed will do what is needed to bring inflation under control.
Colby leads off with the central question of the day: If inflation is so high, why not raise rates today? Warsh stresses that the Fed is committed to bringing inflation down to its 2 percent target and is willing to act to get there. But he doesn’t directly address why policymakers didn’t act today. “If the crux of your question is you haven’t achieved price stability, you’re right,” he says. But he says they are committed to getting there.
As The New York Times first reported earlier this year, Mr. Warsh floated the idea of fewer rate setting meetings in July.
Bottom line: The Fed plans to hold only seven votes on interest rates next year, and six in 2028, down from eight in recent years. Warsh first raised the possibility of reducing the number of policy meetings over the summer.
Stocks are breaking out higher, up roughly 0.4 percent now.
Warsh announces that the Fed will meet eight times next year, as it has in recent years. But in a change, one of those meetings will focus “exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy” and will not include a vote on interest rates. Starting in 2028, the Fed plans to dedicate two meetings to such broader strategy.
All of that strong growth rhetoric has helped push up equity prices again, with the S&P 500 rising 0.2 percent. Bond yields have also continued to push higher, with the 10-year Treasury yield rising to 5.04 percent.

How stocks are trading in the United States
Warsh says that given the strength of the labor market, and the continued elevated rate of inflation, the committee’s discussions focused mostly on the price stability side of the Fed’s dual mandate. That could be a hint that further rate increases remain likely, despite the committee’s decision not to raise rates today.

AI inference infrastructure startup Simplismart has raised $14 million in a Series B funding round led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax.
The fresh funds will be used to strengthen its inference engine and orchestration platform, expand its cloud provider network and support its growth across North America and other global markets.
Entrackr had earlier reported on the deal, which values the company at around $100 million post money. Previously, Simplismart raised $7 million in a Series A round in October 2024.
Founded by Amritanshu Jain, Simplismart provides infrastructure that helps enterprises deploy and run AI models while optimising inference costs, latency and GPU utilisation. Its platform also enables cloud providers to convert their GPU capacity into AI services for enterprise customers.
The company said its annualised revenue run rate grew 14X over the past six months. Its customers include HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema, which use its platform for production workloads across video, voice, multimodal and enterprise AI applications.
Simplismart also works with cloud providers to offer managed AI inference services. At Yotta, its platform powers the serverless inference layer of Shakti Studio, which allows customers to run AI models without managing the underlying infrastructure.
Unlike inference providers that procure or reserve GPU capacity and resell it, Simplismart focuses on the software layer that enables third party GPU infrastructure to support production AI workloads. india-deep-tech-e834ee6dec.headline: German startup NVision shows new path to quantum computing chips in Nature paper
india-deep-tech-e834ee6dec.fulltext:
German startup NVision on Wednesday published a paper in the scientific journal Nature showing a new way to make quantum computing chips that would borrow from the widespread manufacturing techniques currently used in smartphone displays.
Startups and tech giants such as Microsoft and IBM alike are racing to build quantum computers that hold the promise of solving problems that would take conventional machines thousands of years. But NVision, which has raised more than $155 million in funding from firms such as Abbott Laboratories, made the discovery published on Wednesday while working in an entirely different field: improving medical devices.
The company had developed a machine that can zap special sugar molecules until the spin of their electrons aligned. The aligned spins make the sugars a thousand times easier for MRI machines to see, which in turn helps identify cancer cells that eat the sugars far faster than healthy cells.
In the research published Wednesday, NVision showed that its technology can also work on organic molecules similar to those used in organic light-emitting diode (OLED) displays widely used in the electronics business. NVision used AI to simulate hundreds of candidate molecules and then physically synthesized about 40 of them until it found one that could be laid down in a thin layer over a chip made with conventional technology to create a quantum chip.
"We found this 'Goldilocks' molecule," Ilai Schwartz, NVision's chief technology officer, told Reuters in an interview.
NVision also said on Wednesday that it is partnering with US-based chipmaker HyperLight to make its first chips. NVision CEO Sella Brosh said that the company plans to build an entire quantum computer rather than sell only its specialized molecules.
"We want to do the whole thing, to fabricate the chips, to deposit the molecules, to do all the error correction on top of it," Brosh said in an interview. "Eventually, what we will sell is a rack-ready computer."

Nabodita GangulyPublished28 Oct 2026, 08:44 PM IST
Info Edge (India) Ltd, the parent company of recruitment platform Naukri and real estate portal 99acres, announced that Hitesh Oberoi will step down as managing director and chief executive on 2 December 2026, after nearly 27 years with the company.
The company’s board has approved the appointment and redesignation of founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani as executive vice chairman, managing director and group CEO, effective 3 December 2026, subject to shareholder approval.
Bikhchandani said there had been no discussion with the board about appointing an external CEO or whether he would be interim. Oberoi will remain with the company in a non-executive capacity after stepping down from his current position.
“We'll figure out how to evolve the leadership structure at the top going forward. So there's no decision yet on hiring more people. As far as I'm concerned, I'll be taking over. I'll be listening a lot. I'll take Hitesh's guidance. And the good bit is that the leadership below him, who work around him, is very, very good,” Bikhchandani said during the company’s Q2 FY27 analyst call.
However, he acknowledged that he could not continue indefinitely, given his age. “But let the situation stabilize, and then we will see what happens,” he added.
Oberoi will be appointed as an additional director, designated as a non-executive, non-independent director under the promoter category, effective 3 December, subject to shareholder approval, the company said in a statement.
This comes at a time when Info Edge's whole-time director and chief business officer (Naukri) Pawan Goyal has also resigned after seven years with the company to pursue other interests, according to an exchange filing.
Speaking about his reason for leaving, Oberoi said on the analyst call that he had decided to step down after careful consideration to devote more time to his personal interests in education, entrepreneurship, institution-building, investing, and philanthropy, as well as to spend more time with his family.
“For the longest time, I have believed that we have a great team across all our businesses. We have people who have been around for several years. They have grown with the business and matured as leaders. We have a crack team at Naukri and solid leadership at Job Hai, 99acres and Jeevansathi. That is what gave me the confidence to move on,” he added.
Info Edge reported a 12.8% year-on-year increase in standalone revenue from operations to ₹841.7 crore in the second quarter of FY27, from ₹746 crore a year ago, driven by growth in its recruitment, real estate and matchmaking businesses.
However, the company’s net profit fell 92.9% on-year to ₹333.8 crore, compared with ₹4,720 crore in the year-ago quarter. The sharp decline was largely due to an exceptional gain of ₹5,200 crore recorded in the year-ago quarter.
Recruitment remained the company’s largest business, with revenue rising 13.3% on-year to ₹632.3 crore. AI and data products for recruiters and job seekers contributed a high single-digit share of the recruitment business’s top line, with an annualized revenue run rate of around ₹240 crore based on Q2 performance.
The real estate business, 99acres, reported revenue of ₹134.3 crore, up 16.7% from ₹115.1 crore a year ago. The matchmaking business, comprising Jeevansathi and Aisle, recorded revenue of ₹39.5 crore, up 16.5% from ₹33.9 crore in the year-ago quarter.
In contrast, the education business, Shiksha, reported revenue of ₹35.5 crore, down 8.5% from ₹38.8 crore a year ago. The company attributed the pressure to declining referral traffic from Google, which has affected client delivery.

health-tech-ac45c19bd6.headline: Lilly’s retatrutide bests Ozempic on blood sugar, weight loss in phase 3 diabetes showdown
health-tech-ac45c19bd6.fulltext:
Eli Lilly’s triple-G drug candidate retatrutide has beaten Novo’s Ozempic in a head-to-head phase 3 trial, driving deeper reductions in blood sugar and body weight across the 80-week study.
The open-label clinical trial compared two doses of retatrutide—9 mg and 12 mg—to Ozempic 2 mg in almost 1,300 adults with Type 2 diabetes. The participants’ diabetes was inadequately controlled with metformin, with or without a SGLT2 inhibitor. At baseline, the patients’ A1C, a measure of blood sugar, averaged 8.3% and ranged from 7.0% to 10.5%.
After 80 weeks of weekly dosing, A1C had fallen 2.2% in both retatrutide cohorts, compared to 1.8% in the Ozempic arm. The difference was statistically significant, achieving the trial’s primary endpoint.
Participants on 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide lost 19.5% and 20.9%, respectively, of their body weight. Patients receiving Ozempic lost 9.4% of their body weight. With patients on retatrutide losing twice as much weight, the clinical trial hit its key secondary endpoint.
Lilly has yet to share more data from the trial, but teed up a broad attack on Ozempic. The drugmaker reported greater improvements across certain cardiovascular risk factors, including non-HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and systolic blood pressure, with retatrutide than with Novo's drug.
The available safety and tolerability data suggest the benefits come with downsides for some patients. On the top dose of retatrutide, 7.9% of patients discontinued treatment because of adverse events, compared to 2.7% of people on Ozempic.
Rates of diarrhea, nausea and vomiting were higher on retatrutide, at least at the 12-mg dose, than on Novo's drug. The biggest difference was in diarrhea, which affected up to 32.7% and 26.4% of people on retatrutide and Ozempic, respectively. Other safety and tolerability endpoints favored retatrutide. The rate of constipation on Ozempic was 19.8%, compared to up to 14.2% on retatrutide.
The readout adds to the body of evidence that Lilly is building to support retatrutide, an investigational agonist of GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. In March, the drugmaker posted data from a placebo-controlled trial in Type 2 diabetes. Lilly has also delivered data on retatrutide in obesity patients. The company plans to file for FDA approval of the drug candidate in the first quarter of 2027.

global-economics-711bbcf7db.headline: Explained: Why US Fed Reserve decided to not hike rate after FOMC meeting? What Chair Kevin Warsh said in press speech

Explained: The US Federal Reserve maintained the status quo on Wednesday, keeping interest rates unchanged in the 3.75%–4% range despite stubbornly high inflation. The decision was in line with market expectations.
The Fed’s rate decision was approved by a 10–2 vote, with Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack dissenting. While a pause was widely anticipated, the decision raises a key question: with inflation remaining sticky and elevated, why did the Fed not opt for a rate hike instead?
Why did the US Fed Reserve decide to not hike rates after the FOMC meeting?
The Federal Reserve Committee decided to keep the interest rate unchanged in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate. During the press conference, Warsh suggested its policies are already showing signs of having an impact. The FOMC prioritised to continue its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little,” read the FOMC statement.
The “committee will deliver price stability”. The accumulation of more information would aid the FOMC to determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2% goal, mentioned by the US Fed in its statement.
What did US Fed chair Kevin Warsh say?
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh began his post-meeting press conference by noting a number of factors which indicated stronger-than-expected economic activity linked to healthy consumer spending and solid business investment. He underlined that the discussion at this week’s policy meeting remained focused around price pressures.
“It’s our responsibility to get inflation down,” Warsh said. “That’s the reason the FOMC’s discussion over the last couple of days focused mainly on the price stability side of our remit.”
Will Fed rate be hiked in December?
Without giving any clear hint of a US Fed’s strategy for December, Warsh said, “We’ve made clear our readiness to act as circumstances require, and we have shown our willingness to act.”
Politics play no role in Fed decision, says Warsh
The US Fed decision has come just six days before a midterm election, which is likely to revolve around concerns linked to cost of living and affordability. Addressing the press conference, Kevin Warsh rejected the possibility of any influence of politics in the US Fed's decision.
“Politics played no role in the decision," he said at a news conference following the announcement. “I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
Warsh denied that consumers would lose faith in the Fed’s ability to get inflation back to its 2% target, given its decision to forego a rate hike. “There is no soft inflation target," he said.

The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday held interest rates steady, in line with market expectations, days ahead of crucial midterm elections where surging inflation has been a key issue.
The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 to 4.00 per cent, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.
“The accumulation of more information will help the committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the Fed said in a statement announcing its decision.
Two members of the committee, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, calling instead for an immediate 0.25 percentage point rate hike.
The central bank has missed its long-term 2 per cent target for inflation for more than five years, with households and businesses battered by sustained price increases.
US President Donald Trump’s war on Iran, launched in late February, has sent energy prices skyrocketing and fuelled domestic inflation, alongside his wide-ranging tariff policies.
Prices have also been driven by an investment boom in artificial intelligence (AI) technology and the buildout of huge data centres to support it.
The decision comes six days ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party is seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from Trump’s Republicans.
Trump’s handling of the economy has been a key issue throughout the campaign, with working-class households across the country struggling to make ends meet despite largely stable overall economic growth.
US consumer inflation came in hotter than expected in September, clocking in at 3.7 per cent, edging back towards a three-year high established in May.
Still, key policymakers at the Fed – including Warsh – have signalled that they did not see an urgency to raise rates again immediately.
Speaking in Bangkok earlier this month, Warsh said that US economic conditions had “broadly conformed” to policymakers’ expectations, fuelling speculation that the Fed may pause at the October meeting.
On Wednesday, the Fed said economic activity in the United States was expanding at a “strong” pace, upgrading its language from the FOMC meeting six weeks prior.
Wendy Edelberg, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said before the meeting that a decision to hold after raising rates in September was potentially contradictory, given the labour market – the Fed’s other mandate – has been largely stable.
“In terms of the economics of it, I don’t totally understand the logic,” she said.
“If there was a reason to raise interest rates at the last meeting, I think that there’s just as compelling of an economic reason to raise interest rates at this meeting.”
The Fed has a dual mandate to maintain maximum employment while keeping inflation to its long-term target.
It achieves this goal largely using one tool: the economy’s key interest rate. Raising rates tends to cool inflation but can also dampen economic activity; lowering them can spur economic activity but also fuel inflation.
The US unemployment rate has been largely stable around 4.2 per cent over the last year, with job growth mostly in positive territory – albeit driven by a few sectors.
Other advanced economies have also been grappling with high inflation, and on Wednesday Canada’s central bank raised its key rate to 2.5 per cent, its first hike since July 2023.
Loretta Mester, former head of the Cleveland Fed, took part in FOMC meetings during her tenure and insisted that the committee did not “take into account any kind of political issues” when it debated monetary policy.
Still, Trump has loomed large over the Fed since he returned to power last year.
In his second term, he has led an unprecedented assault on the Fed’s independence, pursuing criminal charges against Warsh’s predecessor Jerome Powell and attempting to fire Governor Cook as he demanded lower interest rates.
While the probe against Powell was dropped to smooth the way for Warsh’s Senate confirmation, the White House has recently renewed its drive to fire Cook – despite a Supreme Court decision that batted back an earlier attempt.
“I don’t think it’s going to stop because I think it’s in the nature of this administration to continue those attacks,” Mester said.

global-economics-7bc29a3b31.headline: Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms
global-economics-7bc29a3b31.fulltext:
The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.
Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.
Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.
Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.
During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.
“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.
September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.
Warsh declined to comment on a remark from Donald Trump that, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.
“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.
Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.
Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.
The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.
“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.
Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.
The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.
By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.
“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.
On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.

Google has released its latest frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, offering “significant gains” in coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity. In an announcement on Wednesday, Google highlights Carbon’s top spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v5.0) benchmark, with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra trailing behind.
Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon with a ‘significant leap’ in cybersecurity
Gemini 4 Carbon is outperforming the top models from OpenAI and Anthropic on some benchmarks.
The new Gemini 4 Carbon model offers improvements over Argon, which Google released earlier this month. It’s currently only available to a select group of cybersecurity defense companies, but it will eventually expand to other partners in its Fairwind Program.
The company says Carbon reflects the “pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward,” coming with a “significant leap” in cyberdefense that makes it better at finding vulnerabilities and generating secure code. Carbon currently holds the number one spot on SEC-bench Pro, a benchmark that measures an AI model’s ability to discover real-world bugs, and ExploitGym, which measures how a model can turn a vulnerability into exploits.
Google says Gemini 4 Carbon is built for completing longer tasks, adding that its internal teams have seen it “run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks.” It’s also better at avoiding shortcuts, resisting prompt injection attacks, and collaborating with users, according to Google. Carbon is supposed to offer more “transparency and honesty” as well, by cutting “unsupported claims” by two times when compared to Argon.
It will launch at the same competitive introductory price as Argon, at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
